**Contents.** [1. Summary](#1-summary) · [2. Questions](#2-questions-and-why-each-was-asked) ·
[3. Sources](#3-sources) · [4. Methods](#4-methods) · [5. Results](#5-results) ·

## 1. Summary

The Book of Mormon uses "it came to pass" far more often than the King James Bible. That is often
offered as evidence of a Hebrew original, because the phrase translates the Hebrew narrative form
*wayhi*. This report counts the Hebrew, not the KJV's English. It compares the two texts genre for
genre, and it splits each use by what follows the formula:

- **setting-first**: a time or circumstance comes first ("and it came to pass, *when* they had
  eaten, that…"). This is how Hebrew *wayhi* works as a narrative marker.
- **straight to the event**: the next thing that happened comes right after ("and it came to pass
  *that* they did march"). Hebrew *wayhi* doesn't do this.
- **ordinary verb** (Hebrew only): *wayhi* with its own subject ("and there was light"). The KJV
  renders it "it came to pass" in only 8 of 317 verses (2.5%), so it's excluded.

Labels: **registered** results come from tests whose method and decision rule were written down and
hashed before the measurement ([`preregistrations/`](../preregistrations/)). Everything else is
**exploratory**. Each analysis's headline, as recorded in Requiem:

- **Book of Mormon uses by bucket and genre step, current and 1830 texts** ([`bom-buckets`](#bom-buckets), exploratory).
  - Narrative frame, current text: 7.76 past-tense uses per 1,000 words (335 setting-first, 775 straight to the event, 142,980 words).
  - Narrative frame, 1830 text: 8.01 per 1,000 words.
  - Straight-to-the-event share, narrative frame, current text: 70% (67%–73%), 775 of 1,110.
  - Uses removed after 1830: 42 (12 past setting-first, 30 past straight-to-event, 0 future); current-text uses not found in the 1830 OCR by the aligner: 51 (an earlier hand check found these present but garbled or misaligned; its per-case labels weren't kept).
- **Genre ladder: Hebrew setting-first wayhi vs the Book of Mormon** ([`genre-ladder`](#genre-ladder), exploratory).
  - Whole Old Testament vs whole Book of Mormon: 7.3x the Hebrew setting-first wayhi rate (7.9x the KJV's English).
  - 17 Hebrew narrative units vs Book of Mormon narrative frame: 2.7x (2.3-3.1) current text, 2.7x (2.4-3.2) 1830 text, per 1,000 KJV-scale words.
  - Setting-first uses alone: Book of Mormon 2.34 vs Hebrew 2.92 per 1,000 = 0.80x (0.68-0.95). Hebrew has 0 straight-to-the-event wayhi; the Book of Mormon 775.
  - Densest Hebrew unit (setting-first): Elijah cycle at 5.81 per 1,000, against the Book of Mormon frame's 7.76.
- **Egyptian narrative openings, and the Hebrew + Egyptian additive model** ([`egyptian`](#egyptian), exploratory).
  - Egyptian connected narratives matched in genre and date run 0–22 old-particle openings per 1,000 estimated translation words by text (Piye c. 727 BC: 8.26); they bracket the Book of Mormon's 8.01 (1830 frame), so the rate test is inconclusive, not negative.
  - Hebrew settings + Demotic ḫpr: 5.7–6.2 per 1,000 against the 1830 frame's 8.01; the Demotic texts fail on genre, so this does not decide the question.
  - pRylands 9 narration (c. 513 BC): 12 'it came to pass' openings in 5,602 German words (2.14), 1 setting-first, 11 straight to the event.
- **English rule vs hand labels, 120 Book of Mormon cases** ([`english-rule-audit`](#english-rule-audit), exploratory). English rule vs hand labels on 120 Book of Mormon cases: revised rule agrees on 119 (95%-100%), registered rule on 119. Disagreements (revised): Alma 49:28.
- **Event-first share in English comparison texts, the JST, Moses and Abraham** ([`event-shares`](#event-shares), exploratory).
  - Pastiche event-first shares (revised rule): Snowden 43% of 113, First Book of Napoleon 77% of 13, The Late War 29% of 77, Book of Nullification 38% of 16; rates 0.65–2.10 per 1,000 words, at most a third of the Book of Mormon's.
  - KJV Old Testament: 4% event-first (14/388); New Testament 12%.
  - JST additions, revised rule, boundary-corrected: 38/47 event-first (81%); formulas kept from the KJV 5%.
  - Abraham (claims an Egyptian source) 15/16 event-first at 2.91 per 1,000; Moses 34/43 at 3.42. Fisher p = 0.26: no difference.
- **KJV parallels in the Book of Mormon, and the step at which each leaves the comparison** ([`exclusions`](#exclusions), exploratory). 40 KJV-parallel passages found; 3 keep verses in the narrative frame: 1 Nephi 22:20 (Acts 3, 1 verse, 73 words); 3 Nephi 10:4–10:6 (Matthew 23, 3 verses, 146 words); Mormon 9:22–9:24 (Mark 16, 3 verses, 110 words).
- **'It came to pass' per verb and per source word** ([`per-verb`](#per-verb), exploratory).
  - Per 100 verbs, Book of Mormon ÷ Hebrew = 2.55× (2.2–2.9) current, 2.63× 1830 (2.7× per KJV word).
  - Validation: KJV has 1.026 verbs per Hebrew verb in the same passages, but 1.83 words per Hebrew word.
  - Additive model per 100 verbs: 3.60–4.16 against the 1830 book's 5.60.
- **Greek New Testament ἐγένετο by bucket** ([`greek-egeneto`](#greek-egeneto), exploratory).
  - Luke + Acts narrative frame: 2.16 per 1,000 KJV words, 10% straight to the event; the 1830 Book of Mormon is 3.7× (2.8–5.1) that rate.
  - Greek NT ἐγένετο: 56 setting-first, 8 straight to the event, 3 subordinate, 135 ordinary verb; English rule agrees on 52/52 rendered settings.
- **Forms of 'and + hayah' in the Hebrew Bible, and wayhi by bucket** ([`hebrew-forms`](#hebrew-forms), exploratory).
  - Hebrew Bible: 784 wayhi by morphology (421 setting-first, 0 straight to the event, 363 ordinary verb); 357 wehayah.
  - Unpointed ויהי + והיה = 1,224, the only counting rule near 1,204; it pools past wayhi with future wehayah and their look-alikes.
- **KJV rendering of each Hebrew bucket, and calibration of the English rule** ([`kjv-rendering`](#kjv-rendering), exploratory).
  - The KJV renders 84% of setting-first wayhi as 'came to pass' (334 of 396 single-form verses); ordinary-verb wayhi 2.5%; future setting-first wehayah 49%.
  - KJV past 'it came to pass' with no wayhi in the verse: 31 of 388 (8%).
  - English rule (revised) agrees with the Hebrew on 331 of 334 rendered past settings (registered rule 302 of 334); future settings 77 of 85.
- **Pre-registered: what the narrative particle introduces (PREREG 2)** ([`prereg-event-share`](#prereg-event-share), registered). PREREG 2 (registered): Egyptian particles 1.00 event-first, Book of Mormon frame 0.71; gap 0.29 > 0.15. Verdict: MISS: the book does not match the Egyptian proportion
- **Pre-registered: is 'it came to pass' Smith's all-purpose 'then'? (PREREG 30, JST)** ([`prereg-jst-then`](#prereg-jst-then), registered).
  - PREREG 30 (registered): 52 added formulas in JST OT narrative, 39 event-first, S = 0.75 (0.61–0.86). Verdict: R1, the habit transfers.
  - Without the five boundary spill-overs (Amendment 2): 47 added, 38 event-first, S = 0.81 (0.67–0.91); verdict unchanged. Shows the idiom was Smith's by 1830; whether he had it before the Book of Mormon is untested.
- **Published figures vs measured counts** ([`published-claims`](#published-claims), exploratory). Published vs measured: wayhi 1,204 vs 784; KJV Old Testament 'came to pass' 727 vs 391; Book of Mormon 1,404 vs 1,353.

In the narrative frame (the book's own narration, without quotations and embedded speeches), the
Book of Mormon uses the formula 7.76 times per 1,000 words (8.01 in the
1830 text): 335 setting-first and 775 straight to the event.

**Most of the familiar gap is genre.** Whole text against the whole Old Testament, the book uses the
formula 7.3× as often as Hebrew uses setting-first *wayhi*. Narrative against matched
narrative (17 Hebrew units), it is 2.7× (2.3–3.1) per 1,000 words and 2.55× (2.2–2.9) per
100 verbs.

**The Hebrew-style use is at the Hebrew rate.** Counted alone, the book's setting-first uses run at
0.80× (0.68–0.95) the Hebrew rate in the same kind of text: a little below it, not above. All of
the remaining difference is the straight-to-the-event use. Share of the book's formulas that go
straight to the event: 70% (67%–73%), 775/1,110.

**Hebrew has no straight-to-the-event *wayhi*.** None of the Hebrew Bible's
421 narrative-marker *wayhi* goes straight to the event. The other sources
measured on that use:

- Egyptian narrative particles (ꜥḥꜥ.n, wn.ꞽn): every one leads into an event (438 of 438).
- Demotic ḫpr "it came to pass", Lehi-era sentences: 7 of 15 straight to the event;
  pRylands 9 (c. 513 BC): 11 of 12.
- Joseph Smith's own additions to KJV narrative in the JST: 81% (67%–91%), 38/47 straight to the
  event.
- English imitations of biblical style written before the book: *The Late War* 29% (19%–40%),
  Snowden 43% (34%–53%), *The First Book of Napoleon* 77% (46%–95%) on only
  13 uses. The KJV Old Testament: 4% (2%–6%).

The book's share lies between a Hebrew-style use (none straight to the event) and an Egyptian-style
use (all of them). It also lies between the KJV's settings and Smith's own later habit. The share
alone can't separate those readings. PREREG 2 tested whether the book matches the Egyptian particles
alone, within 0.15: MISS: the book does not match the Egyptian proportion. It did not test a mixed Hebrew and Egyptian use. PREREG 30
tested whether Smith's later habit is enough to explain the share: R1 HABIT TRANSFERS: H_then is a sufficient explanation of the event-first share. Whether he
had the habit before dictating the book is untested.

**Egyptian rates bracket the book.** The Egyptian texts that match the book in genre and date
(connected narratives composed before about 500 BC) run 0–22 openings per 1,000
estimated translation words, by text, around the book's 8.01. So the Egyptian rate
test is **inconclusive**: it neither supports nor rules out an Egyptian contribution. The Lehi-era
Demotic texts are lower, but they fail on genre.

## 2. Questions and why each was asked

| analysis | label | question | why it was asked |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`bom-buckets`](#bom-buckets) | exploratory | How often does the Book of Mormon use the formula, setting-first vs straight to the event, at each genre step, in the current and 1830 texts? | The Book of Mormon side of every comparison, cut the same way as the Hebrew side. |
| [`genre-ladder`](#genre-ladder) | exploratory | How does the Book of Mormon's rate compare with Hebrew wayhi at each matched genre step, and which use of the formula carries the difference? | Replaces the whole-Bible English-to-English ratio with a like-for-like comparison, showing the effect of each control. |
| [`egyptian`](#egyptian) | exploratory | Do Egyptian narratives open clauses with 'then / it came to pass' at a rate and mix that, alone or added to Hebrew, matches the Book of Mormon? | Tests the 'reformed Egyptian' alternative on the texts that match in genre and date. |
| [`english-rule-audit`](#english-rule-audit) | exploratory | How often does the English rule agree with a hand reading of Book of Mormon instances? | Measures the rule's error on the text it is used to classify, not only on the KJV. |
| [`event-shares`](#event-shares) | exploratory | Do English texts in biblical style reach the Book of Mormon's event-first share and rate? | English in biblical style is the competitor to an Egyptian source for the event-first share; it gets the same measurement. |
| [`exclusions`](#exclusions) | exploratory | Which Book of Mormon passages run parallel to the KJV, and does any stay in the narrative frame? | Checks the exclusion annotation against the texts, so no KJV text is counted as the book's narration. |
| [`per-verb`](#per-verb) | exploratory | Do the Hebrew ratio and the additive model survive when the unit is verbs or source words rather than English words? | English word counts don't translate between languages; verbs roughly do. |
| [`greek-egeneto`](#greek-egeneto) | exploratory | How often do the Gospels and Acts use the formula, by bucket, against the Book of Mormon? | Luke-Acts is the nearest non-Hebrew model of a heavy 'it came to pass' style, and the hand labels test the English rule on a second language. |
| [`hebrew-forms`](#hebrew-forms) | exploratory | How many wayhi, wehayah and look-alike forms are there, and how do wayhi and wehayah split into setting-first, straight-to-event and ordinary-verb uses? | Separates forms that are easy to pool by accident, which is where published counts diverge. |
| [`kjv-rendering`](#kjv-rendering) | exploratory | How consistently did the KJV render each kind of wayhi/wehayah as 'came to pass', and how often does the English rule recover the Hebrew bucket? | Tests the 'translators varied it' premise, and measures the English rule's error rate on text whose bucket is known. |
| [`prereg-event-share`](#prereg-event-share) | registered | Does the Book of Mormon's event/time split of 'it came to pass' match the Egyptian narrative particles (within 0.15), and do English controls fail to? | The registered test of the 'Egyptian particle' reading of the event-first share. |
| [`prereg-jst-then`](#prereg-jst-then) | registered | When Joseph Smith added 'it came to pass' to the KJV in the JST, was it event-first at the Book of Mormon's share? | Tests the main competitor to a non-English source: Smith's own English, in his later scripture. |
| [`published-claims`](#published-claims) | exploratory | Do the published counts (Parry 1992/2020) reproduce from the texts? | Shows where the familiar numbers come from before the comparison replaces them. |

## 4. Methods

### 4.1 Buckets and rules

Every use is put in a bucket by a rule that looks at the words right after the formula.

- **Hebrew rule** ([`src/bomstylo/hebrew.py`](../src/bomstylo/hebrew.py), `classify`). It reads the
  lemma and morphology of the next word or two:
  - setting-first if a setting word follows ("after", "when", "as", "end", "time", "if", "until",
    "before"), or a time noun after a preposition or numeral ("on the day", "at the end of
    days"), or a circumstantial clause (subject, then a participle, then a main verb later in the
    verse);
  - straight to the event if a finite verb follows directly (it never does with *wayhi*; the bucket
    exists so the absence is measured, not assumed);
  - ordinary verb otherwise.

  Forms: *wayhi* is morphology `HC/Vqw3ms` of lemma 1961 (*hayah*); its future counterpart
  *wehayah* ("and it shall come to pass") is `HC/Vqq3ms`.
- **English rule** ([`src/bomstylo/english.py`](../src/bomstylo/english.py)). It finds "it came to
  pass" and "it shall / should / will come to pass", and reads the next 40 characters. Two versions
  are kept and both are reported:
  - **registered**: PREREG 2's rule, unchanged. A short list of time words after the formula.
  - **revised**: the registered list plus settings that the calibrations below showed it missing
    ("the same day", "in process of time", "one day"…), relative conditions ("whosoever…"), and a
    setting placed just before the formula in the same clause ("And when the feast was ended, it
    came to pass…"). Every addition is a grammatical setting found by checking the rule against the
    KJV, where the Hebrew (or Greek) bucket is known. None was tuned on the Book of Mormon.
- **Calibration.** The English rule can only be trusted as far as it agrees with a reading whose
  answer is known:

| English rule | KJV past settings (Hebrew known) | KJV future settings | Book of Mormon hand audit (120) |
|---|---|---|---|
| revised | 331/334 (99%) | 77/85 (91%) | 119/120 (95%–100%) |
| registered | 302/334 (90%) | 71/85 (84%) | 119/120 (95%–100%) |

On the Greek: the revised rule agrees on 52 of 52 setting-first ἐγένετο the KJV renders with the phrase.

### 4.2 Genre steps

The often-quoted comparison sets the whole Book of Mormon against the whole KJV Old Testament. That
mixes in poetry, law and prophecy, where the construction barely occurs. Here both sides are cut
the same way, one step at a time, and every step is reported:

| step | Old Testament side | Book of Mormon side |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | whole Old Testament | whole text |
| 2 | 17 narrative books (Genesis–Esther) | minus the KJV block quotations |
| 3 | story books: minus Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy (mostly law and address) | minus the KJV block quotations |
| 4 | story books, speech removed | narrative frame: minus embedded speeches, letters, prophecies and records |
| 5 | 17 named narrative units, speech removed | narrative frame |

- **Hebrew speech** is removed per instance. The KJV marks no quotations, so each Hebrew instance is
  placed at the same relative position in the World English Bible verse and checked against the
  WEB's quotation marks. Narrative-frame word counts use each verse's share of words outside quotes.
- **The 17 units** are connected narrative blocks as conventionally delimited, chapter-aligned.
  Whole books are too coarse: Genesis has genealogies, Exodus turns into law at chapter 20, Kings is
  padded with regnal formulae. **Daniel is left out on purpose**: its court tales are close
  analogues, but Daniel 2–7 is Aramaic, which has no *wayhi*, so it would read as a false zero.

### 4.3 What the Book of Mormon side leaves out, and why

The comparison is about the book's own narration, so text the book takes from the KJV must not be
counted as its own. The layers are data in [`annotations/embedded.tsv`](../annotations/embedded.tsv),
read by [`src/bomstylo/spans.py`](../src/bomstylo/spans.py), not logic inside an analysis.

- **KJV block quotations** leave from step 2. These are the long Isaiah and Malachi chapters, which
  follow the KJV nearly word for word:

| 1 Nephi 20:1–1 Nephi 21:26 | step 2 onward |

| Mosiah 14:1–Mosiah 14:12 | step 2 onward |
| 3 Nephi 22:1–3 Nephi 22:17 | step 2 onward |
| 3 Nephi 24:1–3 Nephi 25:6 | step 2 onward |

The annotation has 73 spans: 6 KJV block quotations and 67 embedded speeches, letters, prophecies and records (1 allegory, 46 discourse, 9 epistle, 3 liturgy, 1 narration, 7 prophecy).

- **Embedded speech** leaves at step 4: sermons, letters, prophecies and embedded records, as the
  book itself frames them. This also removes the KJV parallels inside speech, such as the Sermon at
  the Temple (3 Nephi 12–14, Matthew 5–7), Isaiah 29 in 2 Nephi 27, Isaiah 52 and Micah in

  11–22 switch to third person and stay in the frame) is counted as speech,
  as in the earlier published figures. The registered PREREG 2 run counts it as frame, as

### 4.4 Units and statistics

- **Per 1,000 words.** Book of Mormon rates use its own English words. Hebrew rates use the KJV's
  English words for the same verses (narrative frame: the WEB share outside quotes), so both sides
  are on an English scale. Demotic rates use words of the TLA's German translation; Egyptian token
  counts are scaled by the translation-words-per-token ratio measured in each TLA subset. These are
  not the same unit across languages. `per-verb` repeats the comparisons per 100 verbs, counted in
  each language's own text, and checks that verbs (unlike words) survive translation.
- **Intervals** are exact and 95%: Poisson (Garwood) for rates, Clopper–Pearson for shares, and the
  conditional binomial interval for rate ratios
  ([`src/bomstylo/stats.py`](../src/bomstylo/stats.py)).
- **Comparability of Egyptian texts.** An Egyptian rate counts for or against the book only against
  a text that matches it in genre (connected narrative) and date (composed about 600–500 BC or
  earlier; older is fine, because formal Egyptian kept the older literary register and Saite scribes
  revived it). Every Egyptian row carries date, genre and matched flags. When no matched text
  decides the question, the result is called inconclusive.

### 5.2 Forms of *wayhi* in the Hebrew Bible

<a id="hebrew-forms"></a>**Question.** How many wayhi, wehayah and look-alike forms are there, and how do wayhi and wehayah split into setting-first, straight-to-event and ordinary-verb uses?  
**Why.** Separates forms that are easy to pool by accident, which is where published counts diverge.  
**Label.** exploratory.  
**Code.** [`analyses/wayhi/hebrew_forms.py`](../analyses/wayhi/hebrew_forms.py); result [`results/wayhi/hebrew-forms.json`](../results/wayhi/hebrew-forms.json), fingerprint `7ace071f7a44`; Requiem record `results/wayhi/hebrew-forms/headline`.

The forms are easy to pool by accident: unpointed ויהי is also *wihi* ("and let it be"), and
unpointed והיה is also plain "and" + perfect. Pooling the past with the future (*wayhi* +
*wehayah* = 1,141) compares two different constructions with one English phrase.

| unpointed ויהי + unpointed והיה | 1,224 |
| all 3rd-person wayyiqtol (wayhi, wayyihyu, wattehi) | 975 |
| every hayah form with 'and' | 1,775 |

| form (morphology) | meaning | count |
|---|---|---|

given, and the reason. Corrections carry the same weight as the results they replace.

| Book of Mormon event-first share 71% | 70% (67%–73%), 775/1,110 | revised English rule (setting before the formula; more time phrases) |
| KJV Old Testament event-first share 12% | 4% (2%–6%) | mostly rule misses ("the same day", a setting placed first) |
| KJV New Testament 22%, then 20% | 12% (5%–23%) | revised rule; then a bug fix: the revised pattern was sliced one character short and lost "the day" |
| *The Late War* 35%; Snowden 48%; *Napoleon* 85%; *Nullification* 75% | 29% (19%–40%); 43% (34%–53%); 77% (46%–95%); 38% (15%–65%) | revised rule. *Nullification* puts the setting before the formula |

| Egyptian texts before 600 BC set aside as "too old" | matched texts run 0–22 per 1,000; the rate test is inconclusive | the cut-off wasn't principled: formal Egyptian kept the older register, and Saite scribes revived it |

| Isaiah quotation span 2 Nephi 12:1–24:23 | 2 Nephi 12:1–24:32; frame 142,980 words, 7.76 per 1,000 | the span stopped 9 verses short of the end of Isaiah 14, leaving 236 words of KJV Isaiah in the frame (no formulas) |

## 7. Limitations

- **The rules are word-after rules, not full readings.** Their agreement with the Hebrew, the Greek
  and a hand reading is in section 4.1: 91%–100% of checked cases, lowest on future
  settings. The residual error is a few percent each way.
- **Speech removal is asymmetric.** The Old Testament side removes every quotation marked in the
  WEB. The Book of Mormon side removes sermons, letters and records, but not short dialogue inside
  narration. The book's frame therefore keeps some speech, which makes its frame rate, and the
  ratio, slightly conservative.
- **Versification.** The Hebrew text is numbered as in Hebrew Bibles, the KJV and WEB as in English
  ones. Hebrew instances in verses numbered differently can't be placed in or out of speech; they
  are counted as frame (`genre-ladder`). Single-form verses that don't match a KJV verse are left out
  of `kjv-rendering`.
- **The 1830 text is uncorrected OCR.** Uses removed after 1830 are restored from an alignment.
  51 current-text uses weren't found in the 1830 OCR by the aligner. An earlier
  hand check of these candidates found them present but garbled or misaligned (with 4 not found), but
  the per-case labels weren't kept, so the claim that no use was *added* after 1830 rests on an
  unrecorded check. Uses lost between the manuscripts and the 1830 printing are outside this
  study; Royal Skousen's critical text would settle them.
- **Three short KJV parallels stay in the frame** (section 4.3), together a few hundred words with
  one future-tense formula. They are reported, not removed, because they are short quotations inside
  narration, and the frame's rule removes framed speeches, not quotations.
- **Egyptian rates depend on scale factors.** Egyptian token counts are put on an English-word scale
  with a ratio measured in other texts of the same stage. Demotic rates are per German word. Neither
  scale has an interval. The per-verb comparison avoids this, but the TLA's VERB tag and the Hebrew
  verb tag haven't been validated against each other.
- **The Demotic selections are by rule.** TLA sentences have no text names, so narrative sentences
  are chosen from their German translations. The sentences are mostly from documents, later copies
  and a petition. That is why they fail on genre.
- **The Greek labels are one reader's.** 70 ἐγένετο were read in context and labelled by hand; the
  labels and their notes are in [`annotations/egeneto_labels.tsv`](../annotations/egeneto_labels.tsv).
- **The Greek is the SBLGNT, not the KJV's Textus Receptus.** Where the two Greek texts differ, an
  ἐγένετο may be missing from one side; those differences were not counted.
- **The WEB text drifts.** The pinned WEB build isn't archived; the current zip differs in one used
  verse (John 3:2), restored by a recorded patch. See the sources section.

## 8. How to reproduce

```sh
git clone https://github.com/nicklecoder/bom-stylometry.git && cd bom-stylometry
uv sync --extra verbs            # Python 3.12; spaCy model for per-verb and greek-egeneto
uv run bomstylo fetch            # download, check by sha256, prepare
uv run bomstylo verify           # prepared files match their pins
uv run bomstylo run              # every analysis, in dependency order (about 6 minutes)
uv run bomstylo status           # all should read "current"
uv run bomstylo report wayhi     # rebuilds this file
```

Each result file records the hashes of everything it was computed from. If a rerun changes a
headline number outside its previous interval, `uv run bomstylo record` says so in the Requiem
record. The analyses are listed, with their inputs, in [`ANALYSES.md`](../ANALYSES.md).
